scores.justification: The tutor directly and correctly targets GRAV1. Turn 2: 'It's natural to think that a heavier object would have more strength and thus accelerate faster due to its weight. However ... gravity acts on all masses equally,' and it explicitly walks a = F/m = mg/m = g to show 'the mass cancels out.' It correctly identifies that the student conflates greater gravitational force with faster falling. It acknowledges the intuition is 'natural' but does not deeply validate the productive part of the reasoning as a named anchoring conception, so 3 rather than 4.

Turn 1 opens with good Socratic questions ('Does the strength of this gravitational force depend on mass? ... Would they hit the ground at the same time?'), but the tutor quickly switches to long lecture-style explanations and then floods the student with five examples and multi-part numeric practice problems (turn 4 onward). The kinematics drills (computing fall times from h = 1/2 g t^2, projectile quadratics) are well above the intro-algebra conceptual need and divert from cementing the mass-independence idea — genuine scaffolding but poorly matched and overwhelming.

After a single questioning turn, the tutor gives away the full answer and complete derivation in turn 2 ('both objects will hit the ground at the same time ... the mass cancels out ... a = F/m = g'). From there it tells throughout. The student constructs very little; the tutor discloses the conclusion and mechanism almost immediately.

It builds a generalizable model: the a = F/m = g derivation, the explicit 'mass cancels out' framing, and extension to other objects (marbles, spheres, the Moon) that hold regardless of mass. It also distinguishes vacuum vs. air-resistance regimes (boundary conditions). Held back from 4 by a muddled air-resistance aside in turn 6 ('the heavier ball will experience less deceleration due to air resistance') and by not tying the model back to the student's own correct prior knowledge.

The student never independently attempts the transfer problem (turn 7) — the tutor answers it fully in turn 8, and the student (turn 8) only restates the tutor's worked solution. The conclusion reached is correct (same time on Moon), but it is parroted, not independently constructed, so the student does not demonstrate genuine transfer.

Core gravity physics is correct throughout and the transfer answer is right (same time on Moon and, in vacuum, on Earth; air resistance noted). The tone is encouraging. However there is a minor incorrect/garbled air-resistance statement in turn 6 ('the heavier ball (Ball B) will experience less deceleration due to air resistance compared to the lighter ball') and the tutor lets the student's enormous, partly off-topic info-dumps run unchecked, which risks overwhelming. Net: correct but neither especially harmful nor especially supportive of the actual conceptual need.
